# Wisdom of Solomon Chapter 13 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal)
**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Codex Vaticanus, Wisdom 13 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/WIS_013_page_001.jpg

---

**1** All who were ignorant of God were foolish by nature, and were unable, from the good things that are seen, to know the One Who Is, nor, by attending to his works, to recognize the craftsman.

**2** Instead, they considered either fire, or wind, or swift air, or the circuit of the stars, or the violence of water, or the lights of heaven to be the gods who governed the world.

**3** If, captivated by their beauty, they took these things for gods — let them know how much more excellent than these is their Master; for the Author of beauty created them.

**4** But if they were astonished by their power and their effects — let them understand from these how much more powerful is the one who formed them.

**5** For from the greatness and beauty of created things their Creator is correspondingly perceived.

**6** Yet for these people even so the blame is somewhat less, for they perhaps go astray in their search for God and their desire to find him;

**7** for they live among his works and investigate, and they are persuaded by the sight of what they see, because the things that are seen are beautiful.

**8** But again, they are not to be excused.

**9** For if they had the capacity to know enough to be able to form a judgment about the world, how did they not more quickly find the Master of all these things?

**10** But wretched are those, and in dead things their hopes lie, who called the works of human hands their gods — gold and silver, craft of skill, and likenesses of animals, or a useless stone, the work of some ancient craftsman.

**11** If a woodcutter fells a useful tree and with skill strips off all its bark and trims away its crooked branches, and then works the timber into a vessel fit for daily use,

**12** and the scraps from the woodworking he throws into the fire and cooks himself a meal,

**13** but the remainder that is good for nothing — a crooked piece, full of knots — he takes up in his spare time, and with careful attention carves it into a human likeness by the skill of his experience,

**14** or shapes it to resemble some worthless beast, smearing it with red paint and daubing its surface crimson, covering over every flaw in it with the paint,

**15** and then makes for it a suitable niche and sets it on the wall, fastening it with iron —

**16** he takes care that it should not fall, knowing that it is unable to help itself; for it is only an image and needs assistance.

**17** Yet when he prays about his possessions, his marriage, and his children, he is not ashamed to address a lifeless thing; for health he calls upon the powerless;

**13:18** for life he entreats the dead; for aid he begs the wholly inexperienced; for a journey, something that cannot take a single step;

**13:19** and for profit, business, and success in his undertakings, he asks effectiveness from a thing whose hands have no effectiveness.
